client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. I can't seem to focus on any of my university assignments — I'll sit down to study and just end up staring at the wall for an hour, feeling completely overwhelmed. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, but I didn't know what else to do.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out, especially when you're not even sure it will help — that kind of uncertainty on top of grief is a heavy thing to carry. Losing your grandmother and then trying to function at university sounds genuinely exhausting, and it makes complete sense that your mind keeps drifting when you sit down to study. I'm glad you're here, and I'd love to understand a little more — when you're staring at that wall, what kinds of thoughts tend to be running through your mind in those moments?

client: It's mostly just... her face, honestly. Like I'll be trying to read a paragraph and suddenly I'm just picturing her sitting in her kitchen, and then I feel this wave of guilt because I didn't visit as much as I should have in the last year. And then I spiral into thinking I'm a terrible person, which obviously doesn't help me get back to studying.
therapist: That guilt spiral — going from a tender memory of her in her kitchen straight to "I'm a terrible person" — sounds really painful, and it's such a common but cruel trick our minds play on us when we're grieving. I want to gently notice that feeling guilt about not visiting enough is actually a reflection of how much you loved her, not evidence that you're a terrible person. I'm curious — if a close friend came to you and said they felt guilty about the same thing, what do you think you'd say to them?

client: I know what you're going to say — that I'd tell a friend to go easy on themselves, that they did their best. And yeah, I probably would say that. But it feels completely different when it's me, because I actually know all the times I chose not to go, all the excuses I made, and a friend wouldn't know all that.
therapist: You're right that it does feel different from the inside — you have access to every detail, every moment you second-guessed yourself, and that can make the self-judgment feel more "justified" somehow. But I'd gently ask: would you actually need a friend to have a perfect attendance record to deserve compassion, or is it possible you're holding yourself to a standard you'd never apply to someone you love? What do you think was going on in that last year that made visiting feel harder — was it really indifference, or was life more complicated than that?

client: I hear what you're saying, and yeah, I know logically I wouldn't judge a friend that harshly. But it's different with my dad because I actually had chances to go and I kept putting it off, telling myself there would be more time, and there wasn't. Last year was busy with work stress and I was dealing with my own anxiety stuff, but honestly those feel like excuses when I think about how little time he had left.
therapist: I notice you mentioned your dad just now, where before you were talking about your grandmother — it sounds like there might be layers of loss or complicated feelings here that are all tangled together, and that's worth being gentle with yourself about. What you're describing — telling yourself there would be more time — isn't an excuse, it's something almost every human being does, because we're simply not built to live in constant awareness of loss. I'm wondering, when you call your very real struggles with work and anxiety "excuses," what do you think that says about how much permission you're giving yourself to have simply been a person with your own difficulties last year?

client: I think it says I don't give myself much permission at all, honestly. Like, somewhere in my head there's this voice that keeps saying I should have been able to push through all of that and still show up for her, and anything less than that is just making excuses for being selfish. It's hard to hear you frame it differently, because part of me wants to believe you, but another part feels like if I let myself off the hook, it means what happened with my grandmother didn't matter as much as it should have.
therapist: That last part you said is really important — the fear that self-compassion somehow equals not caring, as if the guilt is the thing keeping your love for her alive. But I'd gently offer another way to see it: the pain you're carrying *is* the evidence of how much she mattered, and you don't need to punish yourself to prove that. What do you think it would actually mean about your love for her if you slowly allowed yourself a little more kindness?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but there's this voice in my head that says if I stop hurting, it means I've moved on, like I've somehow left her behind. And I can't stand the thought of that. What if being kinder to myself just makes it easier to forget her, and then what does that say about me as a daughter?
therapist: There's something really tender in what you just shared — this sense that holding onto the pain is a way of holding onto *her*, like grief has become the last thread connecting you. But I wonder if we could gently challenge that belief together: is it possible that remembering her laugh, her kitchen, the love between you, could keep her present in a way that's actually more alive than guilt ever could be? What are some of the things about her you'd be most afraid of forgetting — not the regrets, but *her*?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that... but it almost feels too easy, like if I let myself just remember the good stuff, I'm somehow letting go of the responsibility I feel for not being there enough at the end. What I'm most afraid of forgetting is the way she hummed while she cooked, this specific little tune she never even realized she was doing, and how she always called me by a nickname nobody else used. But even saying that out loud makes me feel guilty, like I don't deserve to hold those memories warmly when I failed her in other ways.
therapist: The way you just described her — that unconscious little hum, the nickname only she used for you — that's not "the good stuff" as some kind of edited highlight reel, that's *her*, the real her, and the fact that those details are so vivid and precious to you speaks to a relationship that was genuinely full of love. I want to gently challenge the idea that you "failed" her, because the person who failed her wouldn't be sitting here, still aching, still holding onto the exact sound of her humming. What do you think she would say if she could see how tenderly you're still carrying her right now?

client: I don't know... part of me wants to believe she'd say something kind, that she'd tell me I did my best. But there's this other voice that jumps in immediately and says I'm just telling myself what I want to hear, that I'm letting myself off the hook too easily. It's hard to trust the softer version when the guilt has been so loud for so long.
therapist: The fact that the kinder voice is there at all — even if it gets drowned out — matters more than you might realize, because it means some part of you already knows the truth, even if the guilt is louder right now. It makes sense that you'd distrust the softer voice after weeks of the harsh one dominating, but I'd gently ask: what has all that loud guilt actually given you — has it brought you closer to her memory, or has it mostly just kept you staring at walls and unable to study or grieve in a way that feels meaningful? What would it look like to just *experiment*, even cautiously, with letting the kinder voice speak a little longer before the other one cuts it off?

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, when you put it that way, the guilt hasn't really done anything useful. It hasn't made me feel closer to my grandmother or helped me process losing her. It's just been this heavy noise that makes everything harder, and I guess part of me kept thinking if I felt bad enough, it would somehow make up for not visiting her more before she died. But letting the kinder voice stay longer, even as an experiment, feels almost dangerous, like I'm letting myself off the hook too easily.
therapist: You just said something really significant — that you've been using guilt as a form of penance, like feeling bad enough could somehow balance the scales, and recognizing that is a genuinely important shift. "Letting yourself off the hook" implies you did something so wrong it requires ongoing punishment, but what if instead, this is about letting yourself *grieve* — which is actually much harder and more honest than just feeling guilty? I'm wondering, what do you think "making it up to her" could look like in a way that actually honors who she was — maybe something that carries her forward rather than just keeping you in pain?

client: I've been sitting with that word — "grieve" — and it feels heavier somehow than guilt does, which is strange because I thought guilt was the hard part. Guilt at least feels like I'm doing something, like I'm still in it with her in some way, but grief just feels like... accepting she's gone, and I don't know if I'm ready for that. As for making it up to her, I want to believe there's something meaningful I could do, but part of me worries I'd just be turning it into another performance to make myself feel better rather than actually honoring her.
therapist: What you've just named is really profound — that guilt feels like *activity*, like staying connected, while grief feels like surrender, and that distinction makes complete sense when you're not ready to accept the finality of losing her. But I'd gently offer that grief isn't the opposite of being "in it with her" — it's actually the most honest way of acknowledging that she was real, that she mattered, that the loss is real too, and that takes far more courage than guilt does. And that worry about "performing" grief rather than truly honoring her — that kind of self-awareness actually suggests someone who genuinely cares about doing right by her, not someone who's just going through the motions — so I'm curious, when you imagine honoring her in a way that feels *true*, what does your gut say, before the self-critical voice jumps in?
